nameStory: Goat's rue gets its name from its reputation as a plant that goats would eat, though ironically it's actually toxic to livestock! The 'rue' part comes from its somewhat bitter smell when crushed, similar to the herb rue. Some of its other colorful names like 'devil's shoestring' refer to its tough, stringy roots that were once used to make fishing lines.
description: Goat's rue is a knee-high perennial wildflower that looks almost tropical with its feathery compound leaves and clusters of pink and cream pea-like flowers. This native legume typically grows 1-2 feet tall with a somewhat sprawling habit. The whole plant has a silvery, fuzzy appearance due to fine hairs covering the stems and leaves, giving it a soft, velvety texture when touched.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Distinctive two-toned pea flowers with bright pink-purple upper petals and creamy yellow lower petals, clustered at stem tips. The flowers have the classic legume shape with a banner, wings, and keel.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with 10-30 small oval leaflets arranged along a central stem like a feather. The leaflets feel soft and fuzzy due to silvery hairs, and fold up at night or when touched.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing perennial with multiple stems spreading from the base, creating small colonies. The entire plant has a silvery-green, velvety appearance that catches sunlight beautifully.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Flat, hairy seed pods about 2 inches long that turn brown and split open when ripe, revealing small dark seeds inside. Pods are noticeably fuzzy to the touch.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Thick, sturdy stems covered in dense, soft white or silvery hairs that give them a woolly texture. Stems become woody at the base in older plants.

habitat: Look for goat's rue in dry, sandy soils of open woodlands, woodland edges, and clearings throughout New England, though it's more common in southern areas. It thrives in well-drained, acidic soils and partial shade, often growing alongside wild lupine, blueberries, and oak trees. You'll rarely find it in wet areas or deep shade.

seasonality.spring: New silvery-fuzzy shoots emerge from the ground in late spring, with compound leaves unfurling and creating small patches of velvety foliage.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs from June through August, when the showy pink and cream pea flowers appear in clusters at stem tips, followed by developing seed pods.
seasonality.fall: Seed pods mature and split open to release seeds, while the fuzzy foliage may turn yellowish before dying back to the ground.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to underground roots, leaving no above-ground trace until the following spring.

funFact: Despite being called goat's rue and having some common names suggesting it's good animal food, this beautiful wildflower is actually quite toxic to livestock - the roots contain compounds that can cause serious poisoning in cattle and horses, earning it the ominous nickname 'devil's shoestring'!
confusionNotes: The two-toned pink and cream pea flowers are quite distinctive, but the fuzzy compound leaves might be confused with wild lupine at first glance. Remember that lupine has palmate leaves (like fingers on a hand) while goat's rue has pinnate leaves (like a feather), and lupine flowers are solid blue or purple, not two-toned.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse this native goat's rue with the European herb goat's rue (Galega officinalis) sometimes grown in gardens - they're completely different plants in different families. Our native species belongs to a genus called Tephrosia, which means 'ash-colored,' referring to the silvery-gray appearance of the fuzzy foliage.
compareHints: Goat's rue is the only Tephrosia species commonly found in New England, making it unique in the region. Compared to other native legumes like wild lupine or partridge pea, goat's rue stands out with its distinctive two-toned flowers and extremely fuzzy, silvery foliage. While other legumes might have hairy leaves, none have quite the velvety, ash-colored appearance that gives this plant its botanical name.
